# MPM Continuous Emission

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video explains how to continuously emit MPM material to fill a container over time, using the **Overlapping Emission** and **Expansion** features on the MPM Source node. By default, MPM rejects new particles that overlap with existing ones because extra particles in the same voxel add computation cost without improving detail. The expansion parameter injects internal pressure to push existing particles apart, creating voids where new particles can be introduced each substep. This technique is essential for any shot that requires growing volumes of material -- such as filling a glass with liquid or piping whipped cream onto a surface -- and works with any MPM material preset (water, snow, etc.).

## Key Concepts

### [MPM Dual Representation and Particle Density](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=127)
MPM uses a dual representation of voxels and particles. Each voxel typically contains around **8 particles**. Adding more particles beyond this count into a single voxel provides no additional detail -- the particles all contribute to the same voxel, and after the grid-to-particle transfer, they receive identical information back. Extra particles only increase computation cost without improving simulation quality.

### [Default Emission Rejection Behavior](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=159)
By default, when MPM attempts to add new particles during continuous emission, it checks the neighborhood around each candidate particle. If existing particles are already nearby, the new particle is rejected. This prevents wasteful over-packing but also means that a simple continuous emission source cannot fill a container -- it will emit an initial burst and then stop adding material because the emission region is already occupied.

### [Expansion: Creating Voids for New Particles](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=190)
The solution is to push existing particles away from the emission region by sourcing internal pressure. When particles move away, voids open up in the emission neighborhood, allowing new particles to be introduced. By repeating this process on every substep -- push, emit, push, emit -- the volume of material gradually grows outward from the emitter, effectively filling a container.

### [Overlapping Emission and the Expansion Parameter](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=252)
On the **MPM Source** node, enable the **Overlapping Emission** checkbox. This activates the **Expansion** parameter, which controls the amount of internal pressure sourced at the emitter. At an expansion value of **1**, growth is minimal and slow. Cranking the expansion to **25** produces a strong outward push that rapidly displaces existing particles and allows significant continuous emission each substep.

### [Material Versatility](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=314)
Continuous emission expansion is not limited to liquid materials. The video demonstrates switching the MPM material preset from **water** to **snow** and filling the same wine glass geometry. The emission behavior works identically, but the resulting simulation exhibits completely different material properties (cohesion, plasticity, etc.), enabling a wide range of effects from a single workflow.

### [Emission Time Visualization](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=346)
A useful visualization technique involves storing the simulation time (`@Time`) on each particle at emission, then mapping it through a color ramp (e.g., the infrared preset) with wrapping. This produces a layered color visualization where each "generation" of emitted particles receives a distinct color band, making it easy to track how material flows and evolves over time.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Standard setup recipe for MPM simulation | Resolution (increase for fine detail) |
| MPM Source | Defines the emission geometry and behavior | **Overlapping Emission** (checkbox), **Expansion** (default 1; use ~25 for aggressive fill) |
| MPM Collider | Defines collision geometry | Resolution (increase independently), **Particle Level Collisions** (enable for thin colliders) |
| MPM Solver | Runs the simulation | Material preset (water, snow, etc.), Output tab settings |
| Point Wrangle | Custom visualization of emission time | VEX: store `@Time`, map through `chramp()` with wrap |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Set up the scene** -- Create your container geometry (e.g., a wine glass) and your emission source geometry (e.g., a sphere positioned above the container).
2. **Drop MPM Configure** -- Apply the standard MPM Configure recipe to create the solver, source, and collider nodes.
3. **Assign roles** -- Wire the container as the MPM Collider and the emission geometry as the MPM Source.
4. **Increase resolution** -- Raise the resolution on both the source and the collider. For thin colliders like a wine glass, increase the collider resolution directly on the collider node.
5. **Enable Particle Level Collisions** -- On the MPM Collider, enable particle level collisions with the default method to handle thin geometry properly.
6. **Set material preset** -- On the MPM Solver, choose the desired material (water, snow, etc.).
7. **Enable continuous emission** -- On the MPM Source, ensure continuous emission is active (not single-frame).
8. **Enable Overlapping Emission** -- On the MPM Source, check the **Overlapping Emission** toggle to expose the Expansion parameter.
9. **Set Expansion value** -- Start with 1 and increase. A value of **25** works well for aggressively filling a container.
10. **Adjust visualization** -- Set the visualization to display particle speed (0 to 1 range) with a color scheme such as "white water" for liquid, or use a custom emission-time color ramp for debugging.

## Tips & Insights

- With thin colliders such as a wine glass, always enable **Particle Level Collisions** on the MPM Collider node using the default method -- this prevents material from leaking through the walls.
- An expansion value of **1** produces barely visible growth; **25** is a good starting point for filling containers at a reasonable rate.
- The [Cookies and Cream demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=438) shown at the H21 launch used continuous emission expansion specifically for the whipped cream being piped onto the drink. If you need to achieve a similar effect, this feature was designed for exactly that use case.
- Disable the collider visualization to see a transparent version of the container, making it easier to observe the filling behavior.
- Adding more particles beyond ~8 per voxel is pure waste in MPM -- it costs more computation but adds zero detail. The expansion mechanism is the correct way to increase material volume, not increasing particle count.
- You can combine continuous emission with any material preset. Switching from water to snow on the same scene produces a completely different look with no changes to the emission setup.

# MPM Friction and Stickiness

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video covers Houdini 21's new per-voxel varying friction and stickiness on MPM colliders. In previous versions, achieving spatially varying friction required splitting a collider into multiple separate MPM Collider nodes, each with a uniform friction value -- an approach that was cumbersome for complex patterns and added overhead. The new workflow uses a **point attribute** called `friction` (or `stickiness`) on the collision geometry, which the MPM Collider node automatically converts into a VDB grid. This allows arbitrary per-voxel friction and stickiness patterns driven by attributes, groups, painted maps, or any other SOP-level technique.

## Key Concepts

### [Old Workflow: Multiple Colliders](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=2)
In previous MPM releases, varying friction across a single collider surface required physically splitting the geometry into separate pieces, each wired into its own MPM Collider node with a different friction value. For example, to create a ramp with three friction zones (high, zero, high), you would PolyCap the geometry into segments, create three MPM Colliders, set friction to 100 on the outer segments and 0 on the middle, then merge them. This approach becomes impractical for complex friction patterns and adds simulation overhead from multiple collider computations.

### [New Workflow: Attribute-Driven Friction Grid](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=128)
In Houdini 21, you can paint or assign a `friction` attribute directly on the collision geometry at the SOP level. The MPM Collider node detects this attribute and offers a **"Create VDB from Attribute"** checkbox under the **Material Friction** section. When enabled, the node generates a `friction` VDB grid that the solver reads per-voxel during collision evaluation. The same mechanism supports a `stickiness` attribute for varying adhesion.

### [Attribute Type Requirement: Point vs. Primitive](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=223)
The MPM Collider internally looks for a **point attribute** named `friction`. If the attribute exists only as a primitive attribute, the node will promote it from primitive to point, but on low-resolution geometry this promotion averages neighboring values and can collapse all variation into a single uniform value. To work around this on primitive-level attributes, insert a **Cusp** SOP before the collider to split shared points at primitive boundaries, preserving sharp transitions during the promotion. For best results, provide the `friction` attribute as a point attribute from the start.

### [VDB Friction Visualization](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=192)
After enabling "Create VDB from Attribute" on the MPM Collider, you can middle-click the node to verify the `friction` grid exists. The collider node also provides a **Visualize Friction** option to display the friction distribution across the collider surface, which is essential for confirming that the attribute-to-VDB conversion produced the expected pattern.

### [Stickiness Works Identically](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=285)
The same attribute-driven VDB pipeline applies to stickiness. You can vary both `friction` and `stickiness` per voxel on the same collider, providing fine-grained control over how material interacts with different regions of a collision surface.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Standard MPM setup recipe | -- |
| MPM Collider | Defines collision geometry with material properties | **Material Friction > Create VDB from Attribute** (checkbox), **Visualize Friction** (toggle), Friction (uniform fallback), Stickiness |
| MPM Source | Defines emission geometry | -- |
| Point Wrangle | Assign per-point or per-primitive friction values via VEX | `f@friction = value;` based on group membership or other logic |
| Cusp SOP | Split shared points at primitive edges | Used to preserve sharp friction transitions when promoting primitive attributes to point attributes |
| PolyCap | Cap open edges of split geometry | Used in old workflow to separate collider regions |
| Merge | Combine multiple colliders | Used in old workflow only |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Create the scene** -- Set up a collider surface and a source geometry. Drop the MPM Configure recipe as usual.
2. **Assign friction via attribute** -- Add a Point Wrangle (or Attribute Paint, Attribute from Map, etc.) before the MPM Collider input. Write a `friction` point attribute with values between 0 (no friction) and high values like 100 (maximum friction). Use groups, ramps, noise, or any SOP logic to drive the pattern.
3. **Handle primitive attributes** -- If the friction attribute is primitive-level rather than point-level, insert a **Cusp** SOP after the wrangle to split shared vertices. This prevents averaging during the internal primitive-to-point promotion. Verify the point count increases after cusping (e.g., from 260 to over 1000 in the video's example).
4. **Enable VDB generation** -- On the MPM Collider node, check **Create VDB from Attribute** under the Material Friction section. Middle-click the node to confirm a `friction` grid is present in the output.
5. **Visualize and verify** -- Use the **Visualize Friction** option on the MPM Collider to display the friction distribution. Confirm the pattern matches your intent (alternating bands, gradients, etc.).
6. **Optionally add stickiness** -- Repeat the same process with a `stickiness` point attribute for per-voxel adhesion control.
7. **Run the simulation** -- Play the simulation. The first run will compile the OpenCL kernel, which takes extra time. Subsequent runs will be faster.

## Tips & Insights

- Always provide `friction` and `stickiness` as **point attributes** whenever possible. Primitive attributes require a Cusp SOP workaround to avoid averaging during internal promotion.
- The first simulation run after changing the setup will trigger OpenCL kernel compilation, which causes a noticeable delay. This only happens once per session.
- The old method of splitting geometry into multiple MPM Colliders still works but adds overhead and complexity. The attribute-driven approach is strictly superior for spatially varying properties.
- Middle-click on the MPM Collider node to inspect its output and verify that the `friction` grid exists. If you see a uniform value across the entire grid, the attribute is likely being averaged -- check whether you need to cusp or convert to point attributes.
- Friction and stickiness can both vary simultaneously on the same collider, enabling complex material interaction behaviors (e.g., sticky patches surrounded by slippery regions).
- Friction values in MPM are not clamped to 0-1. The video demonstrates values of 0 (no friction) and 100 (very high friction) for clear visual contrast.

# MPM Deforming Colliders

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RylqkW5ePww)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video covers the significantly improved deforming collider support in Houdini 21's MPM solver. In H20.5, deforming colliders had major limitations: stickiness did not work properly, and fast-moving animated geometry would lose contact with material during substep interpolation because the VDB bounding boxes were too tight. Houdini 21 introduces the **"Extend to Cover Velocity"** option on the MPM Collider, which dilates the VDB activation region based on the collider's velocity, ensuring valid SDF and velocity data is available at all substep sample points between integer frames. This fixes stickiness on deforming colliders and enables production-quality interactions like material clinging to a fast-swinging hammer.

## Key Concepts

### [The Deforming Collider Problem in H20.5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RylqkW5ePww&t=2)
In previous Houdini versions, even basic deforming collider scenarios were broken. A simple test -- a sphere pressing down into a box of material and lifting back up -- would fail to exhibit stickiness even with stickiness set to 1. Material would not adhere to the moving collider as expected.

### [Extend to Cover Velocity](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RylqkW5ePww&t=161)
The key new feature is the **"Extend to Cover Velocity"** checkbox on the MPM Collider node. This is now enabled by default in H21. When active, the collider's VDB activation region is expanded (dilated) based on the velocity of the animated geometry. This ensures that when the solver samples SDF and velocity values at substep positions between integer frames, it always finds valid data instead of garbage values from inactive voxels.

### [Why Tight Bounding Boxes Fail at Substeps](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RylqkW5ePww&t=353)
MPM simulations run with many substeps, meaning the solver frequently samples at fractional frame positions (e.g., frame 0.5 between frame 0 and frame 1). With tight bounding boxes:
- At frame 0, the VDB covers only the collider's position at frame 0.
- At frame 1, the VDB covers only the collider's position at frame 1.
- At frame 0.5, the solver tries to interpolate between the two VDBs. If the collider has moved significantly, the sample point may fall **outside both VDBs**, yielding garbage SDF and velocity data on both sides. The interpolation produces meaningless results, and material detaches from the collider.

### [Dilated Activation Region](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RylqkW5ePww&t=478)
With "Extend to Cover Velocity" enabled, each frame's VDB bounding box is expanded to encompass the region the collider will traverse based on its velocity. This means that at any substep between frame 0 and frame 1, the sample point falls within the activated region of **both** VDBs. The solver can then properly interpolate SDF values (knowing the collider's shape) and velocity values (knowing the collider's motion), maintaining correct collision response and stickiness throughout fast animation.

### [Production Example: Crag with Hammer](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RylqkW5ePww&t=99)
The video demonstrates a production-relevant scenario: a character (Crag) swinging a hammer at high velocity through a volume of snow material. The goal is for material to stick to the hammer throughout the swing, including during rapid rotation, and for some material to remain attached even after the fast motion phase. With "Extend to Cover Velocity" disabled, all material detaches during the fast swing section. With it enabled, a substantial amount of material clings to the hammer throughout the shot, with natural trailing and dripping behavior.

|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Standard MPM setup recipe | -- |
| MPM Collider | Defines animated collision geometry | **Type: Deforming/Animated**, **Extend to Cover Velocity** (checkbox, default ON in H21), Friction (e.g., 100), Stickiness (e.g., 100) |
| MPM Source | Defines the material to interact with | Material preset (snow, water, etc.) |
| MPM Solver | Runs the simulation with substeps | Resolution (increase for detail) |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Set up the scene** -- Prepare the animated geometry (the deforming collider) and the source material. The collider can be any animated or deforming geometry -- character meshes, props, etc.
2. **Drop MPM Configure** -- Apply the standard MPM Configure recipe to create the solver, source, and collider nodes.
3. **Set collider type to Deforming/Animated** -- On the MPM Collider node, set the collider type to deforming or animated (as appropriate for your geometry).
4. **Verify "Extend to Cover Velocity" is enabled** -- This should be on by default in H21. If testing the old behavior or troubleshooting, you can toggle it off to compare results.
5. **Set friction and stickiness** -- For maximum adhesion (e.g., material clinging to a fast-moving hammer), set both friction and stickiness to high values such as **100**.
6. **Set the material preset** -- On the MPM Source or Solver, choose the appropriate material (snow, liquid, etc.).

# MPM Continuous Emission

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video explains how to continuously emit MPM material to fill a container over time, using the **Overlapping Emission** and **Expansion** features on the MPM Source node. By default, MPM rejects new particles that overlap with existing ones because extra particles in the same voxel add computation cost without improving detail. The expansion parameter injects internal pressure to push existing particles apart, creating voids where new particles can be introduced each substep. This technique is essential for any shot that requires growing volumes of material -- such as filling a glass with liquid or piping whipped cream onto a surface -- and works with any MPM material preset (water, snow, etc.).

## Key Concepts

### [MPM Dual Representation and Particle Density](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=127)
MPM uses a dual representation of voxels and particles. Each voxel typically contains around **8 particles**. Adding more particles beyond this count into a single voxel provides no additional detail -- the particles all contribute to the same voxel, and after the grid-to-particle transfer, they receive identical information back. Extra particles only increase computation cost without improving simulation quality.

### [Default Emission Rejection Behavior](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=159)
By default, when MPM attempts to add new particles during continuous emission, it checks the neighborhood around each candidate particle. If existing particles are already nearby, the new particle is rejected. This prevents wasteful over-packing but also means that a simple continuous emission source cannot fill a container -- it will emit an initial burst and then stop adding material because the emission region is already occupied.

### [Expansion: Creating Voids for New Particles](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=190)
The solution is to push existing particles away from the emission region by sourcing internal pressure. When particles move away, voids open up in the emission neighborhood, allowing new particles to be introduced. By repeating this process on every substep -- push, emit, push, emit -- the volume of material gradually grows outward from the emitter, effectively filling a container.

### [Overlapping Emission and the Expansion Parameter](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=252)
On the **MPM Source** node, enable the **Overlapping Emission** checkbox. This activates the **Expansion** parameter, which controls the amount of internal pressure sourced at the emitter. At an expansion value of **1**, growth is minimal and slow. Cranking the expansion to **25** produces a strong outward push that rapidly displaces existing particles and allows significant continuous emission each substep.

### [Material Versatility](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=314)
Continuous emission expansion is not limited to liquid materials. The video demonstrates switching the MPM material preset from **water** to **snow** and filling the same wine glass geometry. The emission behavior works identically, but the resulting simulation exhibits completely different material properties (cohesion, plasticity, etc.), enabling a wide range of effects from a single workflow.

### [Emission Time Visualization](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=346)
A useful visualization technique involves storing the simulation time (`@Time`) on each particle at emission, then mapping it through a color ramp (e.g., the infrared preset) with wrapping. This produces a layered color visualization where each \"generation\" of emitted particles receives a distinct color band, making it easy to track how material flows and evolves over time.

# MPM Friction and Stickiness

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video covers Houdini 21's new per-voxel varying friction and stickiness on MPM colliders. In previous versions, achieving spatially varying friction required splitting a collider into multiple separate MPM Collider nodes, each with a uniform friction value -- an approach that was cumbersome for complex patterns and added overhead. The new workflow uses a **point attribute** called `friction` (or `stickiness`) on the collision geometry, which the MPM Collider node automatically converts into a VDB grid. This allows arbitrary per-voxel friction and stickiness patterns driven by attributes, groups, painted maps, or any other SOP-level technique.

## Key Concepts

### [Old Workflow: Multiple Colliders](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=2)
In previous MPM releases, varying friction across a single collider surface required physically splitting the geometry into separate pieces, each wired into its own MPM Collider node with a different friction value. For example, to create a ramp with three friction zones (high, zero, high), you would PolyCap the geometry into segments, create three MPM Colliders, set friction to 100 on the outer segments and 0 on the middle, then merge them. This approach becomes impractical for complex friction patterns and adds simulation overhead from multiple collider computations.

### [New Workflow: Attribute-Driven Friction Grid](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=128)
In Houdini 21, you can paint or assign a `friction` attribute directly on the collision geometry at the SOP level. The MPM Collider node detects this attribute and offers a **\"Create VDB from Attribute\"** checkbox under the **Material Friction** section. When enabled, the node generates a `friction` VDB grid that the solver reads per-voxel during collision evaluation. The same mechanism supports a `stickiness` attribute for varying adhesion.

### [Attribute Type Requirement: Point vs. Primitive](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=223)
The MPM Collider internally looks for a **point attribute** named `friction`. If the attribute exists only as a primitive attribute, the node will promote it from primitive to point, but on low-resolution geometry this promotion averages neighboring values and can collapse all variation into a single uniform value. To work around this on primitive-level attributes, insert a **Cusp** SOP before the collider to split shared points at primitive boundaries, preserving sharp transitions during the promotion. For best results, provide the `friction` attribute as a point attribute from the start.

### [VDB Friction Visualization](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=192)
After enabling \"Create VDB from Attribute\" on the MPM Collider, you can middle-click the node to verify the `friction` grid exists. The collider node also provides a **Visualize Friction** option to display the friction distribution across the collider surface, which is essential for confirming that the attribute-to-VDB conversion produced the expected pattern.

### [Stickiness Works Identically](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=285)
The same attribute-driven VDB pipeline applies to stickiness. You can vary both `friction` and `stickiness` per voxel on the same collider, providing fine-grained control over how material interacts with different regions of a collision surface.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Standard MPM setup recipe | -- |
| MPM Collider | Defines collision geometry with material properties | **Material Friction > Create VDB from Attribute** (checkbox), **Visualize Friction** (toggle), Friction (uniform fallback), Stickiness |
| MPM Source | Defines emission geometry | -- |
| Point Wrangle | Assign per-point or per-primitive friction values via VEX | `f@friction = value;` based on group membership or other logic |
| Cusp SOP | Split shared points at primitive edges | Used to preserve sharp friction transitions when promoting primitive attributes to point attributes |
| PolyCap | Cap open edges of split geometry | Used in old workflow to separate collider regions |
| Merge | Combine multiple colliders | Used in old workflow only |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Create the scene** -- Set up a collider surface and a source geometry. Drop the MPM Configure recipe as usual.
2. **Assign friction via attribute** -- Add a Point Wrangle (or Attribute Paint, Attribute from Map, etc.) before the MPM Collider input. Write a `friction` point attribute with values between 0 (no friction) and high values like 100 (maximum friction). Use groups, ramps, noise, or any SOP logic to drive the pattern.
3. **Handle primitive attributes** -- If the friction attribute is primitive-level rather than point-level, insert a **Cusp** SOP after the wrangle to split shared vertices. This prevents averaging during the internal primitive-to-point promotion. Verify the point count increases after cusping (e.g., from 260 to over 1000 in the video's example).
4. **Enable VDB generation** -- On the MPM Collider node, check **Create VDB from Attribute** under the Material Friction section. Middle-click the node to confirm a `friction` grid is present in the output.
5. **Visualize and verify** -- Use the **Visualize Friction** option on the MPM Collider to display the friction distribution. Confirm the pattern matches your intent (alternating bands, gradients, etc.).
6. **Optionally add stickiness** -- Repeat the same process with a `stickiness` point attribute for per-voxel adhesion control.
7. **Run the simulation** -- Play the simulation. The first run will compile the OpenCL kernel, which takes extra time. Subsequent runs will be faster.

## Tips & Insights

- Always provide `friction` and `stickiness` as **point attributes** whenever possible. Primitive attributes require a Cusp SOP workaround to avoid averaging during internal promotion.
- The first simulation run after changing the setup will trigger OpenCL kernel compilation, which causes a noticeable delay. This only happens once per session.
- The old method of splitting geometry into multiple MPM Colliders still works but adds overhead and complexity. The attribute-driven approach is strictly superior for spatially varying properties.
- Middle-click on the MPM Collider node to inspect its output and verify that the `friction` grid exists. If you see a uniform value across the entire grid, the attribute is likely being averaged -- check whether you need to cusp or convert to point attributes.
- Friction and stickiness can both vary simultaneously on the same collider, enabling complex material interaction behaviors (e.g., sticky patches surrounded by slippery regions).
- Friction values in MPM are not clamped to 0-1. The video demonstrates values of 0 (no friction) and 100 (very high friction) for clear visual contrast.

# MPM Continuous Emission

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video explains how to continuously emit MPM material to fill a container over time, using the **Overlapping Emission** and **Expansion** features on the MPM Source node. By default, MPM rejects new particles that overlap with existing ones because extra particles in the same voxel add computation cost without improving detail. The expansion parameter injects internal pressure to push existing particles apart, creating voids where new particles can be introduced each substep. This technique is essential for any shot that requires growing volumes of material -- such as filling a glass with liquid or piping whipped cream onto a surface -- and works with any MPM material preset (water, snow, etc.).

## Key Concepts

### [MPM Dual Representation and Particle Density](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=127)
MPM uses a dual representation of voxels and particles. Each voxel typically contains around **8 particles**. Adding more particles beyond this count into a single voxel provides no additional detail -- the particles all contribute to the same voxel, and after the grid-to-particle transfer, they receive identical information back. Extra particles only increase computation cost without improving simulation quality.

### [Default Emission Rejection Behavior](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=159)
By default, when MPM attempts to add new particles during continuous emission, it checks the neighborhood around each candidate particle. If existing particles are already nearby, the new particle is rejected. This prevents wasteful over-packing but also means that a simple continuous emission source cannot fill a container -- it will emit an initial burst and then stop adding material because the emission region is already occupied.

### [Expansion: Creating Voids for New Particles](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=190)
The solution is to push existing particles away from the emission region by sourcing internal pressure. When particles move away, voids open up in the emission neighborhood, allowing new particles to be introduced. By repeating this process on every substep -- push, emit, push, emit -- the volume of material gradually grows outward from the emitter, effectively filling a container.

### [Overlapping Emission and the Expansion Parameter](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=252)
On the **MPM Source** node, enable the **Overlapping Emission** checkbox. This activates the **Expansion** parameter, which controls the amount of internal pressure sourced at the emitter. At an expansion value of **1**, growth is minimal and slow. Cranking the expansion to **25** produces a strong outward push that rapidly displaces existing particles and allows significant continuous emission each substep.

### [Material Versatility](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=314)
Continuous emission expansion is not limited to liquid materials. The video demonstrates switching the MPM material preset from **water** to **snow** and filling the same wine glass geometry. The emission behavior works identically, but the resulting simulation exhibits completely different material properties (cohesion, plasticity, etc.), enabling a wide range of effects from a single workflow.

### [Emission Time Visualization](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=346)
A useful visualization technique involves storing the simulation time (`@Time`) on each particle at emission, then mapping it through a color ramp (e.g., the infrared preset) with wrapping. This produces a layered color visualization where each "generation" of emitted particles receives a distinct color band, making it easy to track how material flows and evolves over time.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Standard setup recipe for MPM simulation | Resolution (increase for fine detail) |
| MPM Source | Defines the emission geometry and behavior | **Overlapping Emission** (checkbox), **Expansion** (default 1; use ~25 for aggressive fill) |
| MPM Collider | Defines collision geometry | Resolution (increase independently), **Particle Level Collisions** (enable for thin colliders) |
| MPM Solver | Runs the simulation | Material preset (water, snow, etc.), Output tab settings |
| Point Wrangle | Custom visualization of emission time | VEX: store `@Time`, map through `chramp()` with wrap |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Set up the scene** -- Create your container geometry (e.g., a wine glass) and your emission source geometry (e.g., a sphere positioned above the container).
2. **Drop MPM Configure** -- Apply the standard MPM Configure recipe to create the solver, source, and collider nodes.
3. **Assign roles** -- Wire the container as the MPM Collider and the emission geometry as the MPM Source.
4. **Increase resolution** -- Raise the resolution on both the source and the collider. For thin colliders like a wine glass, increase the collider resolution directly on the collider node.
5. **Enable Particle Level Collisions** -- On the MPM Collider, enable particle level collisions with the default method to handle thin geometry properly.
6. **Set material preset** -- On the MPM Solver, choose the desired material (water, snow, etc.).
7. **Enable continuous emission** -- On the MPM Source, ensure continuous emission is active (not single-frame).
8. **Enable Overlapping Emission** -- On the MPM Source, check the **Overlapping Emission** toggle to expose the Expansion parameter.
9. **Set Expansion value** -- Start with 1 and increase. A value of **25** works well for aggressively filling a container.
10. **Adjust visualization** -- Set the visualization to display particle speed (0 to 1 range) with a color scheme such as "white water" for liquid, or use a custom emission-time color ramp for debugging.

## Tips & Insights

- With thin colliders such as a wine glass, always enable **Particle Level Collisions** on the MPM Collider node using the default method -- this prevents material from leaking through the walls.
- An expansion value of **1** produces barely visible growth; **25** is a good starting point for filling containers at a reasonable rate.
- The [Cookies and Cream demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AGjuRlj5sm4&t=438) shown at the H21 launch used continuous emission expansion specifically for the whipped cream being piped onto the drink. If you need to achieve a similar effect, this feature was designed for exactly that use case.
- Disable the collider visualization to see a transparent version of the container, making it easier to observe the filling behavior.
- Adding more particles beyond ~8 per voxel is pure waste in MPM -- it costs more computation but adds zero detail. The expansion mechanism is the correct way to increase material volume, not increasing particle count.
- You can combine continuous emission with any material preset. Switching from water to snow on the same scene produces a completely different look with no changes to the emission setup.

## Overview

This video covers Houdini 21's new per-voxel varying friction and stickiness on MPM colliders. In previous versions, achieving spatially varying friction required splitting a collider into multiple separate MPM Collider nodes, each with a uniform friction value -- an approach that was cumbersome for complex patterns and added overhead. The new workflow uses a **point attribute** called `friction` (or `stickiness`) on the collision geometry, which the MPM Collider node automatically converts into a VDB grid. This allows arbitrary per-voxel friction and stickiness patterns driven by attributes, groups, painted maps, or any other SOP-level technique.

## Key Concepts

### [Old Workflow: Multiple Colliders](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=2)
In previous MPM releases, varying friction across a single collider surface required physically splitting the geometry into separate pieces, each wired into its own MPM Collider node with a different friction value. For example, to create a ramp with three friction zones (high, zero, high), you would PolyCap the geometry into segments, create three MPM Colliders, set friction to 100 on the outer segments and 0 on the middle, then merge them. This approach becomes impractical for complex friction patterns and adds simulation overhead from multiple collider computations.

### [New Workflow: Attribute-Driven Friction Grid](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=128)
In Houdini 21, you can paint or assign a `friction` attribute directly on the collision geometry at the SOP level. The MPM Collider node detects this attribute and offers a **"Create VDB from Attribute"** checkbox under the **Material Friction** section. When enabled, the node generates a `friction` VDB grid that the solver reads per-voxel during collision evaluation. The same mechanism supports a `stickiness` attribute for varying adhesion.

### [Attribute Type Requirement: Point vs. Primitive](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=223)
The MPM Collider internally looks for a **point attribute** named `friction`. If the attribute exists only as a primitive attribute, the node will promote it from primitive to point, but on low-resolution geometry this promotion averages neighboring values and can collapse all variation into a single uniform value. To work around this on primitive-level attributes, insert a **Cusp** SOP before the collider to split shared points at primitive boundaries, preserving sharp transitions during the promotion. For best results, provide the `friction` attribute as a point attribute from the start.

### [VDB Friction Visualization](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=192)
After enabling "Create VDB from Attribute" on the MPM Collider, you can middle-click the node to verify the `friction` grid exists. The collider node also provides a **Visualize Friction** option to display the friction distribution across the collider surface, which is essential for confirming that the attribute-to-VDB conversion produced the expected pattern.

### [Stickiness Works Identically](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYj3sUThg-0&t=285)
The same attribute-driven VDB pipeline applies to stickiness. You can vary both `friction` and `stickiness` per voxel on the same collider, providing fine-grained control over how material interacts with different regions of a collision surface.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Standard MPM setup recipe | -- |
| MPM Collider | Defines collision geometry with material properties | **Material Friction > Create VDB from Attribute** (checkbox), **Visualize Friction** (toggle), Friction (uniform fallback), Stickiness |
| MPM Source | Defines emission geometry | -- |
| Point Wrangle | Assign per-point or per-primitive friction values via VEX | `f@friction = value;` based on group membership or other logic |
| Cusp SOP | Split shared points at primitive edges | Used to preserve sharp friction transitions when promoting primitive attributes to point attributes |
| PolyCap | Cap open edges of split geometry | Used in old workflow to separate collider regions |
| Merge | Combine multiple colliders | Used in old workflow only |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Create the scene** -- Set up a collider surface and a source geometry. Drop the MPM Configure recipe as usual.
2. **Assign friction via attribute** -- Add a Point Wrangle (or Attribute Paint, Attribute from Map, etc.) before the MPM Collider input. Write a `friction` point attribute with values between 0 (no friction) and high values like 100 (maximum friction). Use groups, ramps, noise, or any SOP logic to drive the pattern.
3. **Handle primitive attributes** -- If the friction attribute is primitive-level rather than point-level, insert a **Cusp** SOP after the wrangle to split shared vertices. This prevents averaging during the internal primitive-to-point promotion. Verify the point count increases after cusping (e.g., from 260 to over 1000 in the video's example).
4. **Enable VDB generation** -- On the MPM Collider node, check **Create VDB from Attribute** under the Material Friction section. Middle-click the node to confirm a `friction` grid is present in the output.
5. **Visualize and verify** -- Use the **Visualize Friction** option on the MPM Collider to display the friction distribution. Confirm the pattern matches your intent (alternating bands, gradients, etc.).
6. **Optionally add stickiness** -- Repeat the same process with a `stickiness` point attribute for per-voxel adhesion control.
7. **Run the simulation** -- Play the simulation. The first run will compile the OpenCL kernel, which takes extra time. Subsequent runs will be faster.

## Tips & Insights

- Always provide `friction` and `stickiness` as **point attributes** whenever possible. Primitive attributes require a Cusp SOP workaround to avoid averaging during internal promotion.

# MPM Deforming Colliders

**Source:** [SideFX MPM H21 Masterclass - Part 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RylqkW5ePww)
**Presenter:** Alex Wevinger

## Overview

This video covers the significantly improved deforming collider support in Houdini 21's MPM solver. In H20.5, deforming colliders had major limitations: stickiness did not work properly, and fast-moving animated geometry would lose contact with material during substep interpolation because the VDB bounding boxes were too tight. Houdini 21 introduces the **"Extend to Cover Velocity"** option on the MPM Collider, which dilates the VDB activation region based on the collider's velocity, ensuring valid SDF and velocity data is available at all substep sample points between integer frames. This fixes stickiness on deforming colliders and enables production-quality interactions like material clinging to a fast-swinging hammer.

## Key Concepts

### [The Deforming Collider Problem in H20.5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RylqkW5ePww&t=2)
In previous Houdini versions, even basic deforming collider scenarios were broken. A simple test -- a sphere pressing down into a box of material and lifting back up -- would fail to exhibit stickiness even with stickiness set to 1. Material would not adhere to the moving collider as expected.

### [Extend to Cover Velocity](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RylqkW5ePww&t=161)
The key new feature is the **"Extend to Cover Velocity"** checkbox on the MPM Collider node. This is now enabled by default in H21. When active, the collider's VDB activation region is expanded (dilated) based on the velocity of the animated geometry. This ensures that when the solver samples SDF and velocity values at substep positions between integer frames, it always finds valid data instead of garbage values from inactive voxels.

### [Why Tight Bounding Boxes Fail at Substeps](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RylqkW5ePww&t=353)
MPM simulations run with many substeps, meaning the solver frequently samples at fractional frame positions (e.g., frame 0.5 between frame 0 and frame 1). With tight bounding boxes:
- At frame 0, the VDB covers only the collider's position at frame 0.
- At frame 1, the VDB covers only the collider's position at frame 1.
- At frame 0.5, the solver tries to interpolate between the two VDBs. If the collider has moved significantly, the sample point may fall **outside both VDBs**, yielding garbage SDF and velocity data on both sides. The interpolation produces meaningless results, and material detaches from the collider.

### [Dilated Activation Region](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RylqkW5ePww&t=478)
With "Extend to Cover Velocity" enabled, each frame's VDB bounding box is expanded to encompass the region the collider will traverse based on its velocity. This means that at any substep between frame 0 and frame 1, the sample point falls within the activated region of **both** VDBs. The solver can then properly interpolate SDF values (knowing the collider's shape) and velocity values (knowing the collider's motion), maintaining correct collision response and stickiness throughout fast animation.

### [Production Example: Crag with Hammer](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RylqkW5ePww&t=99)
The video demonstrates a production-relevant scenario: a character (Crag) swinging a hammer at high velocity through a volume of snow material. The goal is for material to stick to the hammer throughout the swing, including during rapid rotation, and for some material to remain attached even after the fast motion phase. With "Extend to Cover Velocity" disabled, all material detaches during the fast swing section. With it enabled, a substantial amount of material clings to the hammer throughout the shot, with natural trailing and dripping behavior.

## Nodes & Parameters

| Node | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|------|---------|----------------|
| MPM Configure | Standard MPM setup recipe | -- |
| MPM Collider | Defines animated collision geometry | **Type: Deforming/Animated**, **Extend to Cover Velocity** (checkbox, default ON in H21), Friction (e.g., 100), Stickiness (e.g., 100) |
| MPM Source | Defines the material to interact with | Material preset (snow, water, etc.) |
| MPM Solver | Runs the simulation with substeps | Resolution (increase for detail) |

## Workflow Steps

1. **Set up the scene** -- Prepare the animated geometry (the deforming collider) and the source material. The collider can be any animated or deforming geometry -- character meshes, props, etc.
2. **Drop MPM Configure** -- Apply the standard MPM Configure recipe to create the solver, source, and collider nodes.
3. **Set collider type to Deforming/Animated** -- On the MPM Collider node, set the collider type to deforming or animated (as appropriate for your geometry).
4. **Verify "Extend to Cover Velocity" is enabled** -- This should be on by default in H21. If testing the old behavior or troubleshooting, you can toggle it off to compare results.
5. **Set friction and stickiness** -- For maximum adhesion (e.g., material clinging to a fast-moving hammer), set both friction and stickiness to high values such as **100**.
6. **Set the material preset** -- On the MPM Source or Solver, choose the appropriate material (snow, liquid, etc.).
7. **Increase resolution** -- Raise the simulation resolution on the MPM Solver for the level of detail your shot requires.
8. **Run the simulation** -- Play through the frame range. Observe that material now properly sticks to and interacts with the deforming collider during fast motion.
9. **Inspect results at key frames** -- Check frames where the collider velocity is highest to confirm material retention. Compare with "Extend to Cover Velocity" off to appreciate the improvement.

- For maximum stickiness in extreme cases (fast animation, material must cling), set both **friction** and **stickiness** to **100** to give the solver the best chance of maintaining contact.
- The dilated bounding box means more active voxels and slightly higher memory usage, but this is the correct trade-off for physically plausible deforming collider interactions.
- This fix addresses the root cause at the VDB activation level, not just a parameter tweak. Without valid SDF and velocity data at substep positions, no amount of stickiness or friction increase will produce correct behavior -- the solver simply has no meaningful data to work with.
- Before H21, the common workaround for this problem was to manually emit particles along the collider path using continuous emission hacks. This is no longer necessary.
- The improvement applies to all deforming collider scenarios, not just fast-moving objects. Even moderate-speed deformations benefit from more robust substep interpolation.
